summary: Defines new ICMPv6 errors that a network node can send when it drops a packet because of processing limits, such as being unable to handle its headers. Without this, senders get no sign of why packets vanish. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If a post office throws away a parcel because it is too complicated to handle, the sender never learns why. This document lets the post office send back a note giving the reason.

questions: what are the new icmpv6 errors for processing limits
what is icmpv6 headers too long
why are ipv6 packets with extension headers dropped
what is icmpv6 parameter problem code 6
what do icmpv6 codes 5 to 10 mean
subtitle: New ICMPv6 error codes that tell a sender why a router or host dropped its packet for having headers that were too much to process.

tldr.problem: Nodes that cannot process a packet's headers because of processing limits usually drop it silently, so the sender never learns why.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six new ICMPv6 Parameter Problem codes for extension header limits and one Destination Unreachable code, Headers too long, for aggregate header limits, each with a Pointer to the offending octet.
tldr.outcome: Senders and operators get a reason for the loss and a sender may change its headers to avoid repeat drops. The errors are best effort and can be withheld by policy.

today: RFC 8883 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the ICMPv6 specification in RFC 4443.

sections.title: Why Packets Get Dropped Silently
sections.content:
IPv6 carries optional information in extension headers placed between the IPv6 header and the upper-layer header. Many devices limit how much of this they will process, because the headers vary in length, can be long, and can be abused for denial of service. Individual extension headers may be up to 2048 octets long.

When a limit is exceeded the typical behavior is to silently discard the packet. RFC 8883 adds ICMPv6 errors so the discarding node can say why. Six are specific to extension headers; a seventh covers the case where all the headers together exceed what a node can process.

The RFC says sending these errors is RECOMMENDED even when a node drops packets in a way that might be considered nonconformant. The goal is visibility: some reason is better than a silent drop.
sections.eli5: Some routers give up on packets with too many fancy labels and say nothing. This document gives them a polite way to say, "I threw it away because it had too much stuff on it."

sections.title: Where Header Limits Come From
sections.content:
Intermediate nodes such as firewalls often look at extension headers to find the transport header for filtering or connection tracking, even though RFC 8200 says only Hop-by-Hop Options are examined along the path. Hardware devices may have a parsing buffer of a fixed size, such as 64, 128, or 256 bytes, and may lack loop constructs, so a list of options can only be unrolled a fixed number of times.

End hosts are usually software stacks without such inherent limits. Limits there are more likely to be for denial-of-service mitigation or performance, as described in RFC 8504.

The RFC lists trends that make headers longer: deep packet inspection in middleboxes, routing headers such as the one in RFC 8754, in situ OAM headers, and other uses of Hop-by-Hop and Destination Options.
sections.eli5: Some machines can only read a small label on each parcel. If the label is too long or has too many stickers, they cannot finish reading it.

sections.title: Parameter Problem Errors for Extension Headers
sections.content:
The six extension header errors use the existing ICMPv6 Parameter Problem message (Type 4) from RFC 4443, with new Code values 5 to 10. The Pointer field gives the octet offset in the invoking packet where the problem occurred. The message carries as much of the invoking packet as fits without exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU.

  • 5: Unrecognized Next Header type encountered by intermediate node. Sent by intermediate nodes; a final destination SHOULD NOT send it and SHOULD send Code 1 as in RFC 8200 instead.
  • 6: Extension header too big. The Pointer is the first octet of the header that exceeds the limit.
  • 7: Extension header chain too long, meaning the total size in octets is over a limit.
  • 8: Too many extension headers in the chain.
  • 9: Too many options in an extension header (Destination or Hop-by-Hop Options).
  • 10: Option too big, either one option over a length limit or padding options over a limit.

Each of these SHOULD be sent when a node discards a packet for that reason. If the Pointer is used as an offset to read the invoking packet data, a node MUST first check that it is less than the length of that data.
sections.eli5: Each code is a different reason on the note: one label is too long, there are too many labels, or there are too many stickers on one label. A pointer shows exactly where the trouble is.

sections.title: Destination Unreachable for Aggregate Limits
sections.content:
When the combined length of all headers is the problem, the headers may include more than IPv6 headers, for example an encapsulating UDP header. Because Parameter Problem only covers IPv6 headers, the RFC uses ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable (Type 1) with new Code 8, Headers too long.

This message uses the multi-part format of RFC 4884. A new extension object class, Extended Information (Class-Num 4), has a sub-type Pointer (C-Type 1). The object has Length 8, and its Pointer says where the limit was exceeded. The invoking packet data MUST be zero padded to a 64-bit boundary, and to 128 octets if the original was shorter than that.

The error SHOULD be sent when the aggregate header length exceeds a node's limits. It has the lowest precedence: if a packet also matches a Parameter Problem code, that one SHOULD be sent instead.
sections.eli5: When the whole pile of labels is too big, not just one, the router sends a different note saying "headers too long" and points to where it gave up.

sections.title: Priority of Reporting and Host Response
sections.content:
Nodes MUST follow normal ICMPv6 processing from RFC 4443. Only one error SHOULD be sent per packet, so the RFC recommends a priority order, highest first: existing RFC 4443 errors, then Unrecognized Next Header, Extension header too big, Option too big for padding, Option too big for an option length, Too many options, Extension header chain too long, Too many extension headers, and finally Headers too long.

A source host that receives such an error SHOULD validate it, including checking that the packet in the ICMP data matches the upper-layer process or connection that sent it, and SHOULD log it with enough detail for debugging. A host MAY change its use of headers in later packets. For extension header errors, an error SHOULD be reported to an application that enabled extension headers, which may stop using them, change how it uses them, or end communication if they are required.
sections.eli5: If a parcel has several problems, the post office only sends one note, about the most important problem. The sender reads the note, writes it in a log, and may pack the next parcel differently.

sections.title: Reliability and Security
sections.content:
ICMP is unreliable and may consistently fail over some paths, so these errors are best effort and no protocol should rely on their delivery. They can be correlated with other signals such as Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery or Happy Eyeballs for IPv6.

The security considerations of RFC 4443 apply, and firewalls MAY filter these errors in line with RFC 4890. Sending the errors might conceptually be used to covertly deduce the processing capabilities of nodes, so an implementation SHOULD allow a configurable policy to withhold them where ICMP error security is a concern.
sections.eli5: The note might get lost in the mail, so nobody should depend on it. Also, notes can reveal how a machine works, so owners can choose not to send them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned Parameter Problem codes 5 to 10 in the ICMPv6 Type 4 registry, and Destination Unreachable code 8, Headers too long, in the Type 1 registry. In the ICMP Extension Object Classes registry it assigned Class value 4, Extended Information.

IANA also created a sub-type registry for that class, with registration procedure Standards Action. Sub-type 0 is reserved, and sub-type 1 is Pointer.
sections.eli5: The official list of note types was updated so everyone uses the same numbers for the new notes.

items.label: Unrecognized Next Header
items.desc: Unknown Next Header type encountered by an intermediate node.

items.label: Extension header too big
items.desc: One extension header exceeds the size limit.

items.label: Extension header chain too long
items.desc: Total size of the chain exceeds a limit.

items.label: Too many extension headers
items.desc: Number of extension headers exceeds a limit.

items.label: Too many options
items.desc: An extension header has more options than allowed.

items.label: Option too big
items.desc: An option or run of padding options exceeds a limit.
